title: Sriram Raghavan Returns to Noir With New Thriller in the Johnny Gaddaar Mold
excerpt: The Andhadhun director is developing a crime thriller for Matchbox Shots as the production house rides high on Operation Safed Sagar's Netflix success.
body:
• Sriram Raghavan is developing a new thriller in the vein of his 2007 cult classic Johnny Gaddaar, according to a Variety exclusive report.
  • The project is being produced by Matchbox Shots, the Mumbai-based production house behind Andhadhun, Scoop, and IC 814: The Kandahar Hijack.
  • The announcement comes as Matchbox Shots' Operation Safed Sagar, Netflix's most expensive Indian production at Rs 215 crore, climbs the platform's global charts.
  • Raghavan's return to noir territory marks a shift after his 2026 war drama Ikkis, which underperformed commercially despite critical appreciation.

Sriram Raghavan, the filmmaker who defined modern Indian noir with Andhadhun and Johnny Gaddaar, is going back to the genre that made his name. Raghavan is developing a new thriller described as being in the "Johnny Gaddaar zone" for Matchbox Shots, the Mumbai-based production house he has long been associated with, according to an exclusive report by Variety.

Details of the project remain sparse, but the framing signals a return to the tight, twist-laden crime storytelling that earned Raghavan a devoted following. Johnny Gaddaar, his 2007 neo-noir about a young stockbroker who betrays his own gang, drew on James Hadley Chase novels and Vijay Anand's classic thrillers — and has only grown in reputation since its modest theatrical run.

Matchbox Shots on a Roll

The timing is significant. Matchbox Shots' Operation Safed Sagar, a six-episode war drama about the Indian Air Force's role in the 1999 Kargil conflict, premiered on Netflix on August 7 and has since climbed the platform's charts. Made with a budget of Rs 215 crore ($24 million), it is Netflix's most expensive Indian production to date, according to Bloomberg.

The series, directed by Oni Sen and starring Siddharth, Jimmy Shergill, and Abhay Verma, was filmed over 115 days across 11 Indian cities, including at operational IAF bases. Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos said at a screening event that the production contributed over Rs 215 crore to the Indian economy and involved more than 4,000 daily hires.

Sanjay Routray of Matchbox Shots said at the time: "Some chapters in our nation's history demand more than remembrance — they deserve to be brought to life with honesty and scale."

"Some chapters in our nation's history demand more than remembrance — they deserve to be brought to life with honesty and scale."

— Sanjay Routray, Matchbox Shots

Raghavan's Track Record

Raghavan's filmography reads like a master class in suspense. Ek Hasina Thi (2004) put Saif Ali Khan in a revenge thriller. Johnny Gaddaar (2007) reimagined pulp noir for Mumbai. Badlapur (2015) turned Varun Dhawan into a vengeance-seeking widower. Andhadhun (2018), starring Ayushmann Khurrana as a pianist who may or may not be blind, became a global hit and India's entry for the Academy Awards.

His most recent theatrical release, Ikkis (2026), a war biopic about Param Vir Chakra recipient Arun Khetarpal starring Agastya Nanda, drew critical praise but struggled at the box office. At the Red Lorry Film Festival in Mumbai earlier this year, Raghavan was philosophical about the outcome: "When your film doesn't work, you do feel bad. But then, you think of so many great filmmakers whose great films didn't work."

A Busy Slate

Matchbox Shots is not short on projects. The production house has also acquired the screen rights to The Gurugram School Murder, a book by crime journalist Leena Dhankhar about the 2017 killing of a seven-year-old in an elite Gurugram school. Dikssha Jyote Routray of Matchbox Shots is helming that project.

For Indian cinema fans in the diaspora, Raghavan's return to noir is welcome news. His thrillers have consistently traveled well on streaming platforms, with Andhadhun becoming one of the most-watched Indian films on Netflix internationally. A new film in the Johnny Gaddaar mold — taut, clever, and steeped in pulp tradition — could continue that trajectory.
